newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - UK shares brace for Labour victory.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - UK shares brace for Labour victory.

text.p: British equities will be braced next week for the likely return of the first Labour government in 18 years as the lengthy six-week election campaign reaches its climax.

With opinion polls making a victory by the market-friendly ruling Conservatives less likely by the day, market experts on Friday said the best outcome would ironically be the return of a Labour administration with a large working majority.

A small majority or a "hung" parliament in Thursday's poll would by contrast make it more difficult for Labour's centrist leadership to hold its promised strict line on public spending and interest rates, they said.

"The one outcome the markets will not like is Labour winning by a little bit," said Robert Buckland, stock market strategist at HSBC James Capel. "It would mean (Labour leader Tony) Blair would not be able to steamroller the hard left."
After a lengthy pre-election period, in which economic policy has appeared to be in a state of drift, strategists said the smack of firm leadership could be welcomed by the markets.
"We could get a bit of a relief bounce if some of the slightly trickier outcomes don't happen," Buckland said.

Yet the FTSE 100 is unlikely to race away -- since an interest rate rise is expected at a monetary policy meeting due within a week of the poll between the British finance minister and the Bank of England.
Some believe a sharp rate increase of more than a half point is possible as Labour aims to take the heat out of consumer spending and ward off the threat of higher inflation.
"I would not be surprised if Labour decides to take the pain early and agree a half point rise or even more," said Roger Monson, strategist at Daiwa Europe.
"A one point move would wreck the market for about three hours, then people would say maybe they will be held steady for the rest of the year."

A budget is also on the cards if Labour wins, as the incoming administration stamps its own priorities on the running of the economy -- adding to the continuing uncertainties over the economic outlook.
For British markets, the balance of policy is likely to be a key concern as the incoming government aims to cool the economy without damaging industry or unduly squeezing the consumer.

"Barring other influences, I would expect a period of concern over interest rates and whether Labour really will do what it has promised," said Monson, "and the rest of the Spring is going to be bumpy."
Richard Jeffrey, market strategist at Charterhouse Tilney, also highlighted the post-election booby trap awaiting the market in the shape of Labour's finely-balanced rate and tax decisions.

Jeffrey warned that the government's failure to follow up last October's quarter-point base rate rise in effect meant rates would have to be raised yet further in coming months to ensure no pickup in inflation.
"I think political uncertainties will be replaced by uncertainties over economic policy," said Jeffrey, "and they could prove an even greater concern."

Aside from domestic concerns, the influence of New York, often the determinant of overall market trends, could also be felt during the week with Friday's key U.S. employment report likely to be closely studied.
As usual a strong payroll number will rekindle fears of rising interest rates in the world's biggest economy.
"The U.S. payrolls will be the real event of the week for all the markets," said Buckland. "They will be the key numbers."
